# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why1: Right after I named the first step, it makes sense to check how Keel phrased that step before it goes to strangers.
screens.why2: I know what 'a pair' means, but a stranger reading the step has to work out that it means a pair of caption glasses, and 'now' sits awkwardly at the end.
screens.why3: Whether I'd order glasses I can send back is a call a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult can make from their own life.
screens.why4: The drafted line in the box keeps my step, but it drops what the pair is, so the one value shown is a little incomplete.
screens.why5: It still means my 'order a pair with free returns', but leaving out 'glasses' drifts a little from what I typed, and 'most' stretches it to all deaf and hard-of-hearing adults rather than my weekly-conversation segment.
screens.instead: Most would order a pair of caption glasses now, knowing they can send them back free.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (order a pair with free returns), it makes sense to ask whether strangers who like it get a way to raise their hand before the study goes out.
screens.why2: 'Pilot' is everyday startup language to me, and the hint spells out exactly what respondents will see and where I'll find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want emails from deaf and hard-of-hearing people keen to try the glasses is my own call, and I know the answer straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it, and the two are distinct and plainly worded.
screens.why5: My step was 'order a pair with free returns', but the line respondents get is a generic 'Would you try this for real? Leave your email.', so the ask they see is softer than the commitment I typed and doesn't say what trying it means.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order a pair to try, with free returns? Leave your email." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs just before people see the study, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents a spoken interviewer is an odd thing to put first, and the screen does not ask whether a voice suits them at all.
screens.why2: The question is plain, but '400 credits' and 'records the voice you pick once' take a second read, and the hint says voice while my own pick says 'face', so I am not sure which one I am locking.
screens.why3: Picking how my own study reaches my own users is my call and something I know well.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but for deaf people the answer I would want, captions or text first with the voice optional, is not offered, and a 5-second sound sample tells me little about what they will see.
screens.why5: It keeps my wording, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and nothing of AirCaps leaks to the respondent.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults get your questions? Written on screen with captions, voice off (default) / Spoken by Daphne with captions / Spoken by Saskia with captions

screens.why1: This is the right point to choose how strangers answer: the study is built, and the previous screen settled who asks the questions.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to me; I build speech-to-text, so 'catches every spoken answer' and 'where it is loud' are my own trade's terms.
screens.why3: I know my people: many deaf adults won't take an interview asked aloud, and some have speech that recognizers miss, so I can answer this from what I know.
screens.why4: The three choices are distinct and complete, but Daphne's claim to catch 'every spoken answer' is made for typical speech, and the screen doesn't say whether deaf or hard-of-hearing speakers are covered, which is exactly my population.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as I typed them, 'deaf or hard-of-hearing adults', and nothing about AirCaps or the glasses leaks into how they answer.
screens.instead: How should deaf or hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or speak into boxes) / AI interviewer Daphne, questions shown in writing with captions, answers by typing, tapping or talking (speech recognition may miss deaf speech) / Let them choose

screens.why1: Right after choosing how people answer, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: Two of the options are plain, but 'People I found with Keel, from a search on the Contacts page' names a page I never saw in this flow, so I have to read it twice to work out what list it means.
screens.why3: I know who I'd send to: the deaf and hard-of-hearing people I already talk to by name, plus HLAA chapters and online deaf groups where an open link would go.
screens.why4: The three routes (named people, a Keel-found list, one open link posted in a group) are distinct and cover how I'd reach people, and my pick of named people is there.
screens.why5: Nothing here changes what I typed about the wearer or the product, and nothing of AirCaps leaks into how the link is described.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (each gets their own link) · A list I build in Keel's Contacts search (Keel makes a link for each) · A group I'm already in (one open link I post there; each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside the deciding number (1 of 7 lose 12 or more conversations a month, against a bar of 5 of 7), though the verdict line names only Existing sacrifice when Price failed just as flatly at 0 of 7.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows its count over 7 and its bar of 5 of 7, but the tally adds up to five cards numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, so I have to look twice for a missing card 5.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer and Commitment are word for word what I checked, but Existing sacrifice is shown as about 12 conversations a month instead of my $200 to $1,500 a year, and Price is split into $599 plus $20 a month rather than my $599 to $839 a year.
screens.why_b4: The status lines ("smaller than you think", "they value it below your price") tell me which way each belief broke, but nothing says what to do: rethink the price, lead with the free plan, or find who loses more conversations.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but the small sample is never called small, and "6 of 7 would order now" stands as Holding up beside "0 of 7 value it at $599" without any note that the two cannot both be taken at face value.
screens.instead: Not holding up on money: none of the 7 valued AirCaps at $599 and only 1 loses 12 or more conversations a month, yet 6 of 7 said they would order with free returns, so test a lower entry price or the free-captions plan with more than 7 people before trusting the commitment.

screens.why_b1: "Not holding up" sits right beside its deciding count, 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it failed and by how much.
screens.why_b2: Seven people and the bar at 5 are plain, but the unit reads "conversations of the conversations they are in a month" and is printed twice, so it takes a second look to see that the strip counts conversations missed last month.
screens.why_b3: The title is my Existing sacrifice, but I typed $200 to $1,500 a year spent on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras, and the line "about 12 conversations a month" is a number I never wrote, so I only recognise it as the same idea.
screens.why_b4: "They put it below your estimate" plus a pointer to the Price card is generic; it doesn't tell me whether to re-anchor $599 against lost conversations or go after the people who miss the most, like Amaka.
screens.why_b5: n=7 and "a lean, not a call" are on the screen, but the headline "smaller than you think: they lose less today than you estimated" judges my estimate on a measure I never gave, and it talks of "your low" when I gave no range.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean from 7: only Amaka misses 12 or more conversations a month, most miss 2 to 8; your $200 to $1,500 a year was not asked, so check the price against what they pay for captions today.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside the deciding numbers: 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front and 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b2: Both charts show their bands with counts, label my $599 and $20 as band low edges, and show the bar at 5 of 7, so what is counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: I recognise it as my price, but I framed it as $599 to $839 a year with captions free and Pro optional, and the card makes the $20 a month sound required for everyone.
screens.why_b4: The So line repeats the result and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say the concrete thing the quotes show, that people want a trial or demo pair first and that the value sits in the $250 to $599 band.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' is stated; 'Fewer than 2 in 3' is, if anything, softer than the 0 of 7 the data shows.
screens.instead: None of 7 would pay $599 and 6 of 7 put it at $250 to under $599, several only after trying a pair, so test a lower entry price or a loaner/demo, and remember Pro is optional, not part of every price.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Not reached' sits beside '0 of 7 named your price or more · nothing to ask', so I can see at once that this check never ran and why.
screens.why_b2: The bars are all zero and the count line says 7 named less, but the strip shows 5 ghost cells for 7 people, so it takes a second look to see whether that is the bar or the people.
screens.why_b3: Ability to pay was derived by Keel from my $599 and $20 a month against what people spend now; I never typed this line, though I recognise my numbers in it.
screens.why_b4: The So line only says the check waits until 5 of 7 name my price; it doesn't point me back to the Price result, where the real decision about $599 and $20 a month sits.
screens.why_b5: It claims nothing beyond the 7: it says plainly that no one was asked and why, and 'Only 0 of 7' is awkward but not an overstatement.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 would pay $599 and $20 a month (6 named $250 to under $599, 1 under $250), so where the money comes from was never asked; settle the price first, then this can be tested.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7", so I know my belief held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to one question over 7 people, with the four options marked for or against and the bar at 5 of 7 on the strip, so I can read it at a glance.
screens.why_b3: "Buyer and payer" and "The deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else has to agree" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it doesn't tell me what this means for the idea, such as that the payer isn't the problem and the price is, or what to do about the one person, Walter, who needed his wife to agree.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is visible and the screen calls it "a lean, not a call", but the So line's flat "They decide alone on purchases like this" reads firmer than that lean, and "something like this" may refer to cheaper purchases than a $599 pair.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 decided on their own the last time they paid for something like this. That is a lean from 7 people, not a call. Who pays isn't what is blocking you; the price is. Talk to the one whose spouse had to agree before you build anything for a second decider.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '6 of 7 said yes · bar 5 of 7', so I know it held and by how much it cleared.
screens.why_b2: The chart shows 6 for, 1 probably not and 0 no over 7 people, with my bar marked at 5 of 7, and I can see all of that at first look.
screens.why_b3: The title is Commitment and the belief line is the one I checked, 'Most deaf or hard-of-hearing adults would order a pair with free returns now.'
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is an action, but it doesn't say at what price, and the Price card I just read had 0 of 7 at $599, so it doesn't tell me what this yes is worth for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It keeps n=7 visible and says 'a lean, not a call', but 'Book them into it' treats a price-free, free-returns yes as a real commitment, which my Price card says it isn't yet.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would try a pair with free returns, but none valued it at $599. Book them in at the real price and see who still orders before reading this as demand.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the deciding number, '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each'.
screens.why_b3: The $599 and $20 a month are my site's numbers and I recognise them, but I framed price as $599 to $839 a year, and the screen splits it into an up-front price and a monthly fee.
screens.why_b4: The groups point at actions (a loaner pair, multi-speaker pickup), but the screen never says what the failed price means for AirCaps, only the generic 'When a line fails' header.
screens.why_b5: Every count is shown (7 against, 6 asked, Amaka who never saw it), each theme carries only 2 people, and nothing is claimed beyond them.
screens.why_b6: I did not know that people want to borrow a pair even though I already offer 15-day free returns, that big-hall audience questions and eleven-person lunches are the bar, or that single-sided users get by with an end seat; the bands also show most would pay $250 to under $599.
screens.instead: Say plainly that 6 of 7 would order with free returns, yet none values the glasses at $599 and most land at $250 to $599 with under $10 a month: make the free returns read as a borrow-first trial, and test multi-speaker pickup before defending the price.

screens.why1: It's the first thing asked and it checks straight away whether I'm someone who mixes with hearing people, which is obviously why I'd be in this study.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how we say it in the deaf world, and the rest is everyday words I'd get on first read or first hearing.
screens.why3: I know at once whether I talk with hearing people week to week, at work, at the shops, with family.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate with no escape needed, though a lot of my talking with hearing people is by text and I might wonder if that counts.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's "talk with hearing people every week" and nothing about any product reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question with a yes-or-no answer, easy to catch once, if I can lipread or caption the interviewer.
screens.instead: Do you talk face to face with hearing people every week? Yes; No

screens.why1: Right after I say I talk with hearing people every week, it makes sense to show me the idea before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Captions, glasses, lens and eye contact are all words I use every day, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: Losing eye contact while I look down at a caption app on my phone is exactly my life, so I can picture this straight away.
screens.why4: It is a card to read with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea and stays close to captions in glasses, though 'the app on them' is a slightly odd way to say it.
screens.why6: Short, plain sentences with no symbols or brackets that I could follow if it were read out, even if 'inside the lens' is said twice.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, live captions inside your glasses. You wear lightweight glasses, and what the people near you say shows up as captions in the lens. The people building it believe you could read the words and still keep eye contact.

screens.why1: After the idea card, asking how often a conversation gets away from me is an obvious place to start on what it costs me today.
screens.why2: "Miss" is the snag: I catch bits of nearly every conversation and lose the thread of many, so I can't tell if you mean ones I missed whole or ones I only half followed.
screens.why3: It is my life, but nobody keeps a tally of a month's worth of lost conversations, so whatever number I type is a guess.
screens.why4: The number box is fine, but there are three escapes where there should be one, and "I'd rather not say" is a chip that shouldn't exist.
screens.why5: The study is about the last 7 days, but this asks about last month, which drifts from the window that was set.
screens.why6: The stem says well, but "a number of conversations last month, or a low and a high; none is 0" is a mouthful to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, about how many conversations with hearing people did you lose the thread of? (a number box; or say: I can't recall)

screens.why1: Asking what live captions in my glasses would be worth makes sense after the idea card, but the header still says 'What you do today', and this isn't about what I do today, so it lands a bit abruptly.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are plain to me; I know what paying once for the glasses and then a subscription means, because hearing aids and caption apps are sold that way.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and tried caption apps, so I have a feel for prices, but I'd be guessing at the worth of something I've never had on my face.
screens.why4: The bands cover everything and don't overlap, but the $599 edge looks like a price tag someone already picked rather than a round figure I'd think in, and the monthly ladder is fine.
screens.why5: It is clearly the idea being asked about, by the name on the card, with no inside talk about who I am or how they plan to sell it.
screens.why6: Two steps with three bands plus a no is easy to hold, but '$599 to under $1,000' is a mouthful, and 'Or say you can't say' sounds clumsy said out loud.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you to buy outright? Under $500 · $500 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this -- with the escape said as 'Or say I can't say.'

screens.why1: Right after I named a price, it makes sense to ask what would make AirCaps worth more to me.
screens.why2: Plain words I'd use myself, and I can answer it straight off: catching every word in a noisy restaurant, knowing who's talking.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I miss in fast or noisy talk, so I can say what would make it worth more.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps came from the idea card I was shown, and the price band is the one I picked, so nothing new leaks through.
screens.why6: Hearing "two hundred fifty to under five hundred ninety-nine dollars" is a mouthful of numbers, though the question after it is short and clear.
screens.instead: You said about $250 to $600. What would AirCaps need to do to be worth more to you?

screens.why1: After I gave a price and said what would make it worth more, asking who else has a say fits, but it jumps from item 2 of 5 to 4 of 5 and from the money straight to a past purchase.
screens.why2: "Something like this" makes me stop and think whether that means captioning glasses, my hearing aids or a caption app, so I need a second read.
screens.why3: I have never paid for captioning glasses, so I would have to guess whether my hearing aids count, and with those it was really the audiologist and my insurance, not a person agreeing.
screens.why4: The two "yes" options differ only by one person or several and are not listed next to each other, "someone else decided for me" is odd for an adult buying for herself, and my real answers are missing: "insurance or a program had to approve it" and "I've never paid for anything like this."
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks to me, but asking about the last time I paid has drifted from a question about whether I could buy AirCaps myself or would need someone else to agree.
screens.why6: Four options with two near-identical "yes" lines are hard to hold when heard once, and "Or say you can't say" sounds clumsy.
screens.instead: Could you buy AirCaps yourself, or would someone else have to agree? I'd decide on my own · My partner or family would have to agree · Insurance or a program would have to approve it · My employer would have to agree; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: As the last question after the idea and the price, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually order a pair, though the 'What you do today' kicker doesn't match a what-would-you-do question.
screens.why2: 'Order a pair with free returns' is plain to me, and with 'live captions inside the lens' just above it I know a pair means glasses.
screens.why3: Whether I'd order captioning glasses I could send back is a choice I can make myself, since I'm the one who misses conversations at dinners and at the theatre.
screens.why4: The scale is lopsided: there is a firm yes, a probably not and a no, but no 'probably yes', which is where a lot of us would land when we want to try them before we trust them.
screens.why5: It keeps to the idea card's own words and says nothing about the company's plans or how it labels people like me.
screens.why6: One short question with three options I can hold, though the first option repeats the whole question back to me.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order a pair with free returns, or not? Yes · Probably yes · Probably not · No
